title: How Search and Rescue Dogs Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain search and rescue (SAR) dogs: their two-part job of finding people and alerting their handler, the difference between tracking (scent-trail) dogs and air-scent dogs, specialties such as cadaver, water, avalanche, wilderness and urban disaster dogs, the positive-reinforcement training process (about 600 dog hours and roughly 1,000 handler hours), the demanding certification levels including urban tracking tests, and the handler's on-call life and navigation duties. The episode closes with a listener mail about Pando, the aspen clone in Utah, and recommendations for nature ambience audio.

segments.title: Opening banter and episode setup
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck welcome listeners, introduce guest producer Andrew, and say this episode follows up on an earlier search and rescue episode and a promised look at search and rescue dogs. They joke about their own dogs and a UK trip.

segments.title: What SAR dogs do and time pressure
segments.summary: SAR dogs are working dogs whose two jobs are finding people and alerting their handler. Time is critical in missing-person, collapse and avalanche cases, and handlers are on call around the clock.

segments.title: Dog sense of smell and human scent
segments.summary: Dogs have a sense of smell far stronger than humans and can detect scent underwater or at a distance. The hosts discuss skin cell scent particles (rafts) that people shed, and why bloodhounds are associated with tracking.

segments.title: Tracking dogs versus air scent dogs
segments.summary: The two general categories of SAR dogs are tracking (trailing) dogs, which follow a specific person's scent from a last known point, and air scent dogs, which search broadly by picking up airborne scent. Tracking dogs must arrive before searchers contaminate the trail. Breeds like German shepherds, Labs and border collies are suited to the work, and bloodhounds' ears and facial folds help concentrate scent.

segments.title: Specialties: cadaver, water, avalanche, urban
segments.summary: Specialties include cadaver dogs trained to find human remains, water dogs for drowning victims who must ride boats and helicopters, and urban disaster dogs, the most demanding type, of which only about a hundred in the US are qualified. Trainers use artificial scent such as Sigma Pseudo Corpse Scent. Evidence dogs find clothing or items in crimes.

segments.title: Basic obedience, distraction tests and certification levels
segments.summary: Training starts with basic obedience and temperament, then a test where a dog must stay while the handler leaves and other handlers take over. The third level is physical agility: tunnels, steep inclines, cherry pickers, helicopters and boats. Urban tracking is the hardest final test, with a track of half a mile to a mile through a city and a thirty-minute wait before the dog starts.

segments.title: Reward-based training and avalanche training method
segments.summary: Trainers identify each dog's favorite reward and use it consistently. Avalanche training starts with the handler hiding in a snow hole, then increases hide time up to about ten minutes. Dogs learn to find people for play or treats, even at disaster scenes. Training of the handler, including navigation and first aid, is also covered, along with the time required for dogs and humans.

segments.title: Dog career arc and breed history
segments.summary: Urban disaster dogs are typically younger and retire to less demanding wilderness work. Adoption is common after retirement. The hosts briefly discuss a future episode on dog origins and joke about the film Water World.

segments.title: Listener mail about Pando
segments.summary: A listener from Colorado whose family camps near Fish Lake, Utah, writes about Pando, the aspen clone, its grazing fences and threats, and recommends nature ambience audio. Josh and Chuck mention a Lawson Barney art account on Instagram.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh gives the website and email contact information and signs off.
